q8.answer: The older run keeps waiting with no lock held, and its 72-hour approval clock keeps running. When it gets approval and takes the production lock, the superseded check compares its commit with production's current_tag; if production already runs a newer commit, the run ends quietly with no announcement. Whether a waiting approval should be cancelled as soon as a newer run reaches staging is an open question that I did not decide.

q9.answer: An approved run that gets the production lock outside the window releases it and waits, holding no lock, for the next window, which opens Monday 09:00 UTC; the window is checked after the lock is taken, so a deploy cannot start after 15:00. How a run waits when another production deploy holds the lock (queue order, timeout, retry) was never decided; I only relied on the CI named lock, so that part is undecided.

q10.answer: The watch starts when deploy.sh canary reports the canary ready, and runs for 15 minutes. Every 30 seconds it reads the canary 5xx ratio and the canary's request count over the last minute from Prometheus. A failure is a usable sample (at least 100 requests) with a 5xx ratio above 1%, which aborts at once, or three unusable samples in a row, which also abort; if neither happens over 15 minutes, the run promotes. Whether unusable samples should also count toward the 1% limit is still open.

q11.answer: The plan only says the run waits at a CI manual approval job restricted to release-approvers, which records who approved and when. It does not say how approvers are notified that a run is waiting, since the #deploys announcements cover only failures, expiries and finished production deploys, and it does not specify what information approvers see beyond the author rule. I did not decide this.

q12.answer: For production, a failed stable rollout is not rolled back with deploy.sh rollback, because previous_tag holds an older version than the one to restore; instead the run redeploys the current_tag read from SSM at run start, then runs canary-off, and pages a human if that recovery fails. For staging, a failed deploy.sh staging run ends and leaves the environment as the script left it, with no automatic return to a known image; I chose that because failed deploys are not rolled back automatically, and whether that is acceptable is an open question. The production recovery side effect (previous_tag gets overwritten with current_tag) is also still open.
